Day 45 of 100 · Linux Administration

systemd

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

systemd manages service lifecycle, dependencies and startup state so long-running processes are supervised rather than left to terminal sessions.

Architecture / mental model

unit file → systemd manager → process lifecycle + dependencies + restart policy

How it works

Service units describe how a process starts, stops and relates to other units. `systemctl` talks to the service manager rather than manipulating the process directly.

`enable` controls whether a unit is wanted during boot; `start` controls the current runtime state. They are separate operations, which is why `enable --now` is useful when both are intended.

Restart policies can improve resilience but also hide crash loops. A service that restarts forever is not healthy simply because `systemctl` keeps producing a PID.

Hands-on reference

systemctl status SERVICE
systemctl cat SERVICE
sudo systemctl enable --now SERVICE
journalctl -u SERVICE -b

Verification

Inspect the effective unit, start/restart it, then confirm both process state and application behavior. Reboot testing is the evidence for boot-time expectations.

Field note / gotcha

`active (running)` means systemd has a running process, not that the application can satisfy a real request or reach its dependencies.

Security considerations

Use unit hardening options where appropriate, run services under dedicated users and keep Environment files or credentials permissioned correctly.

What I learned

A service manager supervises processes; health still belongs to the application path.
